reconcile.connective: Adam Clarke insists the effect is a real, if unexplained, natural process — not a miracle — and would recur under similar conditions.

discrepancy.connective: Skeptic Steve Wells presses the objection bluntly: the text credits striped rods with determining offspring coloring, which is simply bad biology.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, comment on Genesis 30:39 (skepticsannotatedbible.com/gen/30.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; gen/30.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It has long been an opinion that whatever makes a strong impression on the mind of a female in the time of conception and gestation, will have a corresponding influence on the mind or body of the fetus. This opinion is not yet rationally accounted for. It is not necessary to look for a miracle here; for though the fact has not been accounted for, it is nevertheless sufficiently plain that the effect does not exceed the powers of nature; and I have no doubt that the same modes of trial used by Jacob would produce the same results in similar cases.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Clarke directly defends the rod trick's implied mechanism (visual impression shaping offspring appearance) as a genuine, if unexplained, natural law rather than superstition or miracle — the strongest period engagement with the exact claim skeptics call bad biology.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Genesis 30:37-41
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke treats this exact passage directly, arguing the rod trick's effect is a real natural process science had simply not yet explained, not a false or miraculous claim.

link.title: Did Jacob placing branches in front of his flock really result in the offspring being speckled and spotted?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment arguing the rods alone did not cause the coloring and crediting divine intervention instead, per Jacob's own account in Genesis 31:10-12.
